# Introduction

I want to determine a humbly-optimized strategy for my long-term investment portfolio.

My goal is to maximize the [utility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility) I will derive from this portfolio. Assuming constant relative risk aversion and a utility function of following form, as per [Merton's portfolio problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merton's_portfolio_problem):

$$
u(x) = \frac{x^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
$$

where

- $u(x)$ is the utility derived from an $x$ level of wealth (which is consumed to produce utility)
- $x$ is the amount of wealth consumed
- and $\gamma$ is a constant measuring the level of risk aversion

I estimated that, personnally, $\gamma = 2$. This estimation is out of the scope of this study, see Haghani & White ([2018](https://elmwealth.com/measuring-the-fabric-of-felicity/)) for an introduction.

@fig-crra-utility shows the shape of my utility function: utility rises with consumed wealth but with decreasing marginal return, and $\gamma$ sets how fast that marginal rate of return decays.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crra-utility
#| fig-cap: "CRRA utility of consumed wealth, for my $\\gamma = 2$ and two other risk aversion levels, for comparison. (Utility is ordinal -- only the curvature and the comparison of values are meaningful, not the values alone.)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 400)
crra_gammas = [(1.5, "#E69F00", 1.2), (2.0, "#0072B2", 2.2), (3.0, "#009E73", 1.2)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for gamma, color, linewidth in crra_gammas:
    ax.plot(
        x,
        x ** (1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma),
        color=color,
        linewidth=linewidth,
        label=f"γ = {gamma:g}",
    )
ax.set_xlim(x.min(), x.max())
ax.set_ylim(-3, 0.15)
ax.set_xlabel("Wealth consumed, x")
ax.set_ylabel("Utility, u(x)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

I am designing this strategy to be implemented in an [Interactive Brokers (IBKR) *compte-titre ordinaire* (CTO)](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/accounts/individual.php?menu=B) as a French citizen. This choice implies that I would have access to a wide array of instruments.

I have already defined the universe of assets I will consider and submit to the optimization (all EUR-denominated):

- an [MSCI ACWI](https://www.msci.com/indexes/index/892400/msci-acwi-index) ETF;
- a global, government, EUR-hedged bond ETF such as [DBZB](https://etf.dws.com/en-gb/LU0378818131-global-government-bond-ucits-etf-1c-eur-hedged/);
- a [managed futures](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/White-Papers/Understanding-Managed-Futures) ETF such as [DBMFE](https://www.imgp.com/fund/LU2951555403-imgp-dbi-managed-futures-fund-r-eur-ucits-etf/) (ideally, several ones to diversify the manager risk);
- and a gold ETF.

The definition of this universe is out of scope but was inspired, between others, by Ilmanen ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198)).

An IBKR CTO allows the implementation of short box spreads for fixed-rate, low-cost leverage. The derivation of the properties of this combination of options is fascinating but also kept out of the scope of this study, see [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_spread).

Analytical process:

- I will first define the inputs of the optimizer -- the assets' expected return, volatility and correlation. This step is very challenging, hence, I will employ techniques designed to keep those estimates humble and as evidence-based as possible.
- I will then run mean-variance optimization (MVO) on those inputs to identify the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio), as per the modern portfolio theory. MVO being theoretically exact but practically very sensitive to the fraction of error in the inputs, I will correct this result by tilting the assets' weights toward a conservative anchor.
- Finally, I will solve for the amount of leverage to apply to this optimized portfolio to maximize utility.

To summarize, the challenge is to estimate the portfolio of assets that will maximize the expected return per unit of risk taken, and then leverage it to the level of risk that best suits my psychology (@eq-challenge).

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{return}}{\text{risk}}}_{\text{to maximize}} \times \underbrace{\text{leverage}}_{\text{to adapt to my risk aversion level}}
$$ {#eq-challenge}

The SG CTA Index is the live, net-of-fee return of a [pool of the largest managed-futures CTAs](https://wholesale.banking.societegenerale.com/fileadmin/indices_feeds/SG_CTA_Index_Constituents.pdf). # Computing the inputs of the mean-variance optimizer
## Covariance matrix

The first input we will tackle is the covariance matrix.


### Historical covariances & Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage

```{python}
#| label: ledoit-wolf
import numpy as np

from covariance import ledoit_wolf_covariance, correlation

cov_lw, delta = ledoit_wolf_covariance(returns)
lw_delta_fmt = f"{delta:.2f}"

# Shrinkage target: the average of the off-diagonal sample correlations.
sample_corr = returns.corr()
off_diagonal = ~np.eye(len(sample_corr), dtype=bool)
avg_corr_fmt = f"{sample_corr.values[off_diagonal].mean():.2f}"
```

The sample of historical returns allow us to compute a covariance matrix. But, as per Ledoit & Wolf, [2003](http://www.ledoit.net/honey.pdf), "obody should be using the sample
covariance matrix for the purpose of portfolio optimization" because of its estimation error. As such, our sample covariance matrix is shrunk toward a constant-correlation target with the optimal shrinkage constant $\delta$ set to `{python} lw_delta_fmt` by the Ledoit-Wolf estimator. That results in each pair-wise correlation coefficient to be pulled toward the average sample pair-wise correlation coefficient (@tbl-shrinkage). The problem targetted by Ledit & Wolf is most important in cases where the number of assets surpasses the number of observations in each returns time series which is far from our case, by we apply that method for robustness.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shrinkage
#| tbl-cap: "Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk covariance matrix."
correlation(cov_lw).round(2)
```

@tbl-shrinkage-shift shows how much the shrinkage moved each correlation (shrunk - sample) toward the `{python} avg_corr_fmt` average.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shrinkage-shift
#| tbl-cap: "Shifts caused by the Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage over the covariance matrix."
(correlation(cov_lw) - returns.corr()).round(3)
```


### Regime inspection

The correlations above -- sample or shrunk -- are full-period averages.
They hide the evolution of the degree of comovement over time between the sleeves. The optimizer relies on covariances to find the best combination of assets (diversification) and maximize risk-adjusted returns.
To be more specific, I want equities to be un- or anticorrelated relative to the other sleeves when equities crash. A negative average correlation doesn't provide enough time granularity to examine this.
So it is important that we scrutinize those single numbers before feeding them to MVO. In @tbl-regime-corr, I bucket the 304 months by the sign of the equity return and compute each sleeve's correlation with equity within each bucket.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-regime-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation with equity by equity-state bucket."
from regimes import conditional_correlations

conditional_correlations(returns).round(2)
```

@tbl-regime-corr tells a different story than the average:

- Bonds have been a risk-off hedge: increasingly negatively-correlated as equity weakens (down to -0.17 in the worst quartile).
- Trend acted as a convex hedge: mildly positively-correlated with equity when equity rises (0.13), but turning slightly negative when equity falls (-0.06 to -0.09).
- Gold acted as a tail hedge: roughly uncorrelated when equity rises or falls modestly, but negative (-0.17) in the worst quartile.

The buckets in @tbl-regime-corr are static -- they pool months regardless of when they occured. @fig-rolling-corr instead shows how equity correlated with the other sleeves over the period, on a 36-month rolling window.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rolling-corr
#| fig-cap: "36-month rolling correlation of each sleeve with equity."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from regimes import rolling_correlations

roll = rolling_correlations(returns)
colors = {"bonds": "#0072B2", "trend": "#009E73", "gold": "#E69F00"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for sleeve in roll.columns:
    ax.plot(roll.index, roll[sleeve], color=colors[sleeve], linewidth=1.5, label=sleeve)
ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Correlation with equity")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

@fig-rolling-corr makes the instability even clearer.

- As the [headlines](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/A-Positive-Stock-Bond-Correlation-Is-a-Terrible-Reason-to-Add-More-Equity-Risk-to-Your-Portfolio) said, the stock-bond correlation turned positive. It was negative for most of the period, but flipped sign around 2022 and reached a peak (in our sample) at +0.71 in 2025. The risk-off hedge of the 2000s and 2010s has, for now, become a risk-on co-mover.
- Trend's correlation to stocks swings widely (from +0.77 in 2006 to -0.33 in 2024), consistent with its convex, regime-dependent profile.
- And gold's was most stable (-0.34 to +0.37) albeit rarely substantially anticorrelated.


### Cautious overrides

The regime inspection makes me distrust one correlation (even shrunk): the equity-bonds one. Its 25-year average is roughly zero, but it flipped positive in 2022, peaked near 0.7 in 2025, and is still elevated (~0.5) at the sample end (@fig-rolling-corr). Feeding the optimizer a diversifying ~0 would let it lean on a bond hedge that I don't trust going forward. So I override it to a conservative 0.25 -- above the historical average, below the current regime -- and leave the other five correlations at their shrunk levels.

I distrust bonds historical volatility for the same reason. Its 3.8 % sample figure leans on the structurally calm ZIRP/QE decades (2001-2019 ran ~3.0-3.1 %), but the post-2020 volatility regime has run at or above 5 %, the 36-month rolling vol now sits near 5.0 % (@fig-rolling-vol), and the ETF's own 3-year factsheet standard deviation is 4.48 % ([IGLE factsheet, iShares](https://www.ishares.com/uk/individual/en/products/310297/ishares-global-govt-bond-ucits-etf-eur-hedged-dist-fund)). So I raise it to 5 %. (This is a load-bearing input for the bond weight givne by MVO: the tangency's bond weight falls from ~68 % to ~53 % and equity doubles.)

The non-equity sleeves' crisis-hedging value, which a single matrix cannot see, is not preserved here by editing the correlations. Instead, it will be handled downstream by the risk-parity anchor.


@tbl-final-corr & @tbl-final-vol show the correlations & volatilities MVO will be fed.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Final correlation matrix (equity-bonds overridden)."
from covariance import annualized_vols, final_covariance

rho_equity_bonds = 0.25
sigma_bonds = 0.05
cov_final = final_covariance(returns, rho_equity_bonds=rho_equity_bonds, sigma_bonds=sigma_bonds)
correlation(cov_final).round(2)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-vol
#| tbl-cap: "Final annualized volatilities (bond vol overridden to 5%)."
pd.DataFrame({"annualized vol": annualized_vols(cov_final).map("{:.1%}".format)})
```


## Expected returns

The optimizer's second input is the expected-return vector -- the least reliable MVO input, and the one that most wrecks the weights when it is off. So rather than feed it my own point estimates directly, I pass them through a [Black-Litterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black%E2%80%93Litterman_model) model: start from the return the *market* implies (the equilibrium prior), then tilt toward each of my views only as far as my confidence in it warrants. That shrinkage toward the market *is* the humility mechanism -- a mistaken or over-confident view is pulled back toward the market, not taken at face value.

### The equilibrium prior

Reverse optimization recovers the market's own expectations: if investors hold the cap-weighted portfolio $w_\text{mkt}$, and hold it optimally under a risk aversion $\delta$, the returns they must expect are $\Pi = \delta\,\Sigma\,w_\text{mkt}$. The weights come from market capitalizations (all in USD -- only the ratios enter):

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-prior
#| tbl-cap: "Market caps, the implied market weights, and the equilibrium prior Π (real)."
import black_litterman as bl
from black_litterman import MARKET_CAPS, market_weights

bl_prior = bl.equilibrium_prior(cov_final)
bl_delta = bl.market_delta(cov_final)
bl_delta_fmt = f"{bl_delta:.1f}"
_caps = pd.Series(MARKET_CAPS).reindex(cov_final.index)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "cap (USD tn)": _caps.map(lambda x: "--" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:,.1f}"),
        "market weight": market_weights(cov_final.index).map("{:.1%}".format),
        "prior Π": bl_prior.map("{:.2%}".format),
    }
)
```

The caps are the MSCI ACWI free-float market cap (equity, \$101 tn), the FTSE WGBI-Developed index *market value* (bonds, \$31 tn) and WGC financial gold (\$15 tn), each from its 2026 factsheet. Managed futures is a **zero-net-supply** strategy with no market capitalization, so it takes weight $0$ in the market portfolio; its prior then falls out of the reverse-opt as $\beta_\text{MF}\times\text{premium}\approx 0$ (near-zero because it is near-zero-beta), and its return enters entirely as a view.

$\delta$, the market's risk aversion, I derive from an **independent** external equity risk premium -- deliberately *not* from my own views, which would make the prior a circular mirror of them. An arithmetic, over-bills, world equity premium triangulated across the [DMS/UBS 2026 Yearbook](https://www.ubs.com/content/dam/assets/wm/static/cio/documents/giry2026-summary-public.pdf), [Damodaran](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histimpl.html) (implied US 4.23 %), [Kroll](https://www.kroll.com/en/reports/cost-of-capital/recommended-us-equity-risk-premium-and-corresponding-risk-free-rates) (5.0 %) and the [Fernandez 2026 survey](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6570342) (5.5 %) lands at ~5.0 %; blended to a market-portfolio premium (bond term premium ~1 %, gold ~0) and divided by $\sigma^2_\text{mkt} = w_\text{mkt}'\Sigma\,w_\text{mkt}$, this gives $\delta \approx$ `{python} bl_delta_fmt`. $\delta$ scales the prior's level -- and, downstream, the leverage -- but not its composition.

### My views

Each sleeve's view is an honest from-source estimate (Ilmanen's per-asset method), carried into BL with an Idzorek confidence in $[0, 1]$ set by how far I trust it against the prior:

- **Bonds -- ~1.2 % real, confidence 0.7.** DBZB's index, the FTSE World Government Bond Index - Developed Markets, yields 4.08 % to worst at 6.49 years effective duration ([FTSE](https://research.ftserussell.com/Analytics/Factsheets/Home/DownloadSingleIssue?issueName=WGBIDM&IsManual=true), 2026-07-26); hedging to EUR costs ~0.9 pp^[Hedging a foreign bond to EUR gives up the currency-weighted foreign-minus-EUR short-rate differential (covered interest parity). This 0.9 pp is napkin math: the index is ~40 % USD, where that differential is currently ~2 pp, partly offset by its lower-rate JPY sleeve. It shifts the real figure by only ~±0.2 pp.], leaving ~3.2 % hedged nominal; minus ~2 % expected inflation ([ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/ecb_surveys/survey_of_professional_forecasters/html/ecb.spf2026q3.en.html)) gives ~1.2 % real. The starting yield is a strong forward predictor of bond returns and the CAPM prior is a weak model for bonds, so I lean on the view.
- **Equity -- 4.03 % real, confidence 0.8.** Elm Wealth's all-world payout-adjusted cyclically-adjusted earnings yield (P-CAEY; White & Haghani, [2024](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4874559)) -- a direct forward real-return estimate -- at **4.03 %** (2026-06-30, [Elm Wealth](https://elmwealth.com/capital-market-assumptions/)). Held firmly: it is forward and valuation-aware, whereas the prior is valuation-blind and higher.
- **Trend -- ~1.8 % real, confidence 0.6.** No yield to anchor on, so the historical mean of the live proxy (Ilmanen's fallback): the SG CTA Index compounded 3.8 % nominal EUR over 2000-2026; minus ~2 % expected inflation gives ~1.8 % real. Lower confidence -- a backward-looking mean with no forward anchor -- but the momentum literature and independent estimates keep the sleeve meaningful.
- **Gold -- no view.** No cashflow and no forward anchor (long-run real return $\approx$ inflation), so I express nothing and leave gold at its equilibrium prior.

### The posterior

Black-Litterman blends each view with the prior in inverse proportion to their uncertainties (Idzorek's confidence method, $\tau = 0.05$):

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-posterior
#| tbl-cap: "Black-Litterman prior, view, confidence, and posterior μ (real). Gold has no view, so its posterior is the prior."
from black_litterman import VIEW_CONFIDENCES
from mu import VIEWS_REAL

bl_post = bl.posterior_returns(cov_final)
_rows = {}
for _a in cov_final.index:
    _has_view = _a in VIEW_CONFIDENCES
    _rows[_a] = {
        "prior Π": f"{bl_prior[_a]:.2%}",
        "view": f"{VIEWS_REAL[_a]:.2%}" if _has_view else "--",
        "confidence": f"{VIEW_CONFIDENCES[_a]:.1f}" if _has_view else "--",
        "posterior μ": f"{bl_post[_a]:.2%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(_rows).T
```

This posterior is the MVO input. Equity stays near my view (my 0.8 confidence in a valuation-aware number disciplines the market's higher prior); bonds are shrunk only modestly (0.7 confidence holds the yield-based view well above the CAPM prior); trend is pulled part-way down from 1.8 % toward its near-zero prior; and gold, viewless, sits at its equilibrium value.


# Determining the portfolio weights

With the posterior $\mu$ (@tbl-bl-posterior) and the covariance $\Sigma$, the risky portfolio is their max-Sharpe -- the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio). Mutual-fund separation then applies: since short box spreads lend at ~the risk-free rate, every investor holds this same risky book and scales it by leverage to their own risk appetite (the next section; remember @eq-challenge?). Black-Litterman has already done the humbling -- the posterior is shrunk toward the market -- so I take the tangency directly, with no further shrinkage or blend.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-risky
#| tbl-cap: "The risky portfolio: max-Sharpe of the BL posterior on the study covariance (real, financed at $R_F$ = 0.19 %)."
from composition import portfolio_performance, tangency_weights

w_risky = tangency_weights(cov_final, bl_post)
r_risky, s_risky, sh_risky = portfolio_performance(w_risky, bl_post, cov_final)
_weights = ((w_risky * 100).round(1).astype(str) + " %").to_frame("risky portfolio")
_stats = pd.DataFrame(
    {"risky portfolio": {"E[r]": f"{r_risky:.1%}", "σ": f"{s_risky:.1%}", "Sharpe": f"{sh_risky:.2f}"}}
)
pd.concat([_weights, _stats])
```

Equity and bonds anchor the book at ~41 % each, with trend (~9 %) and gold (~8 %) as the diversifiers. Bonds sitting level with equity is the honest consequence of a high (0.7) confidence in a yield-based view the market prices too low, not a thumb on the scale; and gold earns its ~8 % from its equilibrium prior and diversifying covariance alone, no view required.


# Applying leverage

The risky portfolio's volatility (~7 %) is far below the risk I should bear given its Sharpe. Financing at a real rate $R_F$ -- my box-spread cost, ~0.19 % real^[Box spreads finance at ~the EUR risk-free curve at their tenor. Rolling quarterly, that tenor is ~3 months, well approximated by the overnight €STR of 2.19 % ([ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/financial_markets_and_interest_rates/euro_short-term_rate/html/index.en.html), reference 2026-07-24); minus ~2 % expected inflation gives ~0.19 % real. The truest figure is the implied rate of my own box fills each quarter -- this is the ex-ante proxy.] -- a CRRA investor with risk aversion $\gamma$ holds a fraction $k^* = S / (\gamma\,\sigma)$ of wealth in the risky portfolio, where $S = (\mu_p - R_F)/\sigma$ is its excess Sharpe and $\sigma$ its volatility. That implies a target volatility $\sigma^* = S/\gamma$ and an expected real return $R_F + S^2/\gamma$; $k^* > 1$ is gross leverage, financed by short box spreads at ~$R_F$.

```{python}
#| label: leverage-calc
#| include: false
from leverage import (
    GAMMA,
    levered_allocation,
    levered_expected_return,
    optimal_leverage,
    target_volatility,
)

k = optimal_leverage(sh_risky, s_risky, GAMMA)
k_fmt = f"{k:.1f}×"
sstar_fmt = f"{target_volatility(sh_risky, GAMMA):.1%}"
erlev_fmt = f"{levered_expected_return(sh_risky, GAMMA):.1%}"
```

At $\gamma = 2$ that is a gross exposure of `{python} k_fmt`, a target volatility of `{python} sstar_fmt`, and an expected real return of `{python} erlev_fmt`. @tbl-leverage shows the resulting book as fractions of NAV: the financing leg (`cash/borrow`) is the box-spread borrowing.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage
#| tbl-cap: "The risky portfolio levered to the CRRA optimum (γ = 2), % of NAV."
pd.DataFrame(
    {"% NAV": (levered_allocation(w_risky, k) * 100).round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + " %"}
)
```

The resulting $k^*$ is `{python} k_fmt`. But this is the unconstrained optimum, and a practical cap (portfolio margin, box-spread capacity) may bind below $k^*$ and would tilt the book away from the low-vol sleeves. The real financing rate above already trims $k^*$; any box-spread spread over the risk-free would trim it a little more. @tbl-leverage-gamma shows the sensitivity to $\gamma$.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage-gamma
#| tbl-cap: "Leverage, target volatility, and expected real return vs. risk aversion γ."
rows = {}
for g in [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0]:
    rows[g] = {
        "k* (leverage)": f"{optimal_leverage(sh_risky, s_risky, g):.2f}×",
        "σ* (target vol)": f"{target_volatility(sh_risky, g):.1%}",
        "E[r] real": f"{levered_expected_return(sh_risky, g):.1%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.rename_axis("γ")
```
